title: Power Banks: How Much Capacity Do You Actually Need?
metaDescription: How to calculate the power bank capacity you actually need based on your phone's battery, why the advertised mAh isn't what you actually get, and 10000mAh vs 20000mAh compared.
author: ByteBuy Team

sections.content: The number on a power bank's box is the most misleading spec in consumer electronics, and not because of false advertising — it's just physics. A "20000mAh" power bank will not give your phone 20000mAh of charge. Understanding why is the difference between buying the right capacity and buying twice the power bank you actually needed, or worse, half.

sections.title: Why Advertised mAh Isn't What You Get

items.label: Voltage Conversion Loss
items.value: Power banks store energy at ~3.7V but output at 5V/9V — converting between them loses roughly 20-30% of capacity

items.label: Real-World Output
items.value: A 20000mAh power bank realistically delivers 13000-15000mAh usable to your phone

items.label: Phone Battery Sizes
items.value: Most phones: 3000-5000mAh. A 20000mAh bank realistically charges a phone 2.5-3 times, not 4-5

items.label: Output Wattage
items.value: Determines charging speed, not capacity — check this separately if fast charging matters to you

items.label: LED Indicator
items.value: Shows the power bank's own remaining charge, not how much it can still deliver to your device

pros: 10000mAh is genuinely enough for most people's actual use case — a full extra charge for a typical phone with some left over, in a pocket-friendly size
20000mAh covers multi-day trips, camping, or charging a phone and a second device (earbuds, tablet) without needing a wall outlet at all
USB-C input/output on current models means one cable charges the bank and your phone, no separate charger cable needed
LED battery indicators, even basic ones, are genuinely useful for knowing when to recharge the bank itself before you need it
cons: The voltage conversion loss (roughly 20-30%) applies no matter which capacity you buy — it's not a defect, budget for it when calculating what you need
Bigger capacity means bigger and heavier — a 20000mAh bank is a real pocket/bag presence, not something you forget you're carrying
Generic, unbranded power banks (common at this price tier) vary more in real-world quality and longevity than named brands — check recent buyer reviews, not just the spec sheet
Output wattage, not just mAh, determines whether it can fast-charge your specific phone — check that separately before assuming a high-capacity bank charges quickly

items.question: How do I calculate what power bank capacity I actually need?
items.answer: Take your phone's battery capacity (check its specs, typically 3000-5000mAh), divide the power bank's advertised mAh by about 1.5 to account for voltage conversion loss, then divide that by your phone's capacity to get realistic full charges. A 20000mAh bank divided by 1.5 gives roughly 13000mAh usable — enough for about 3 full charges on a 4000mAh phone, not 5.

items.question: Is a 20000mAh power bank worth it over a 10000mAh one?
items.answer: If you're charging one phone for a day or two away from an outlet, 10000mAh covers that in a smaller, lighter package. Go to 20000mAh if you're traveling multiple days, charging more than one device, or want a real buffer margin rather than cutting it close on a single trip.

items.question: Why did my power bank charge my phone less than the advertised mAh suggests?
items.answer: This is expected, not a fault — power banks store energy at a lower internal voltage than the 5V or 9V they output to charge your phone, and that conversion loses roughly 20-30% of the rated capacity. A 20000mAh bank realistically delivering 13000-15000mAh to your phone is normal, not a sign of a defective unit.

items.question: Does power bank output wattage matter as much as capacity?
items.answer: For charging speed, yes — capacity only determines how many charges you get, not how fast each one happens. If your phone supports fast charging and the power bank's output wattage is too low, you'll still get a full charge, just slower than plugging into a wall charger. Check both specs if speed matters to you.

sections.content: Buy capacity based on the math, not the biggest number on the box. Work out how many charges you actually need between outlets, account for the roughly 20-30% conversion loss every power bank has, and pick accordingly — 10000mAh for daily topping-up, 20000mAh for multi-day trips or charging more than one device. Anything beyond that is paying for size and weight you probably won't use.
